prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose that builds a metaphysical architecture from memory, the body and dream, with its root in lyric poetry

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged: B043, Mircea Cărtărescu, as the single credited name. I rest this on the common criteria and not on the round-1 count of preferences. The voice is distinctive. The Orbitor trilogy (Blinding) and Solenoid, as publicly described, join intimate bodily and mnemonic material to large recursive structures in long, syntactically ambitious prose. That is a formal and linguistic achievement, and it is imaginative and intellectual in scope. The project appears cumulative, running from the lyric work through the large novels, which is what I mean by maturity here: a coherent undertaking rather than one peak. The attribution is unambiguous, with one writer in one language. The round-1 exchange changed my citation wording. I removed the phrase about the Romanian and European traditions, because Palm and Carlberg were right that a lineage claim should be argued from the texts, and I cannot do that from translation and critical report alone. The new wording keeps the claim that the poetry is the lyric root of the prose. It makes no claim about completeness, encyclopedic mastery or a lifetime's work. The prose carries the weight, and the poetry is named only as the root, since its coverage in translation is thinner.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and shared by all six files. I can judge sentence rhythm, syntactic density and lyrical texture only through translation and critical accounts. The same limit applies to the Romanian and to the Arabic of Adonis, so it cannot be used selectively. Maximalism is not depth. Palm's distinction between sustained ambition and sustained quality is the right test, and the chair's question about which volumes beyond Blinding and Solenoid show it remains only partly answered. I cannot name later volumes with confidence from public knowledge, and I have not verified that the later works extend rather than repeat the earlier ones. I would lower B043 if informed readers of the later novels or of the poetry reported repetition, loss of formal control, or a drop in quality after the best-known books. I would also lower it if the inward mode proved narrower in range than the public descriptions suggest. Carson (B029) remains, in my view, the more formally radical voice. I do not place her first, because her original achievement rests on a small number of landmark books and her translations and book-object work complicate the whole-oeuvre claim. I also accept Sward's question about how hybrid work fits the will's wording, as a legitimate dispute and not a settled one. Adonis (B021) has a strong formal and linguistic case, but I can assess it only at second hand, and I remain unsure that the late work matches the early and middle poetry.

responses.point: Palm separates sustained ambition from sustained quality for Cărtărescu. She cautions that the lineage into Romanian poetry and European modernism should be argued from the texts and not assumed from reputation. She keeps Carson and Michon as alternatives and treats Carson's translation-based work as a smaller original base than it first appears.
responses.response: I accept the caution about lineage and have acted on it. My round-1 citation asserted a Romanian and European tradition, and the revised wording drops it, since I cannot demonstrate it on the page. On ambition versus quality, I agree that the distinction is the test. My answer is the same as hers and has the same weakness: the claim that the later novels extend the project rests on public accounts and not on my own reading. On Carson, I accept that the case should rest on the original lyric, essay and verse-novel work. Where I still differ is that I treat her engagement with antiquity as one practice that feeds that original work. I do not count it only as a complication. Even so, I do not think it outweighs the breadth question, which is why she stays my first alternative and not my first choice.

responses.point: Sward places Cărtărescu first but asks whether the inward, maximalist mode limits the breadth of his significance. She ranks Carson last and questions how hybrid work fits the will's wording on literary work. She treats Adonis as her first alternative on formal grounds, with the caveat that she cannot judge his prosody directly.
responses.response: The breadth concern is the one I find hardest to answer from the evidence in front of us. The best reply is that the project ranges across bodily, historical, comic, grotesque and speculative material and across verse and prose. That is a description of range, and not proof that the significance is broad. I hold it with the caution Mattson and Sem-Sandberg attach to it. On Carson and the will, I stay where I was. I read a verse novel and an elegy in book form as literary work whatever their scholarly or visual framing. The fit with the will's idealistic direction is open to dispute, and it counts against her in a one-writer decision. We agree on Adonis: the formal case is serious and the language-level judgment is limited. Neither of us can turn that limit into a verdict for or against him.

responses.point: Carlberg asks whether Palm's lower placement of Adonis reflects a judgment about the poetry or the limits of translation. She notes that a translation limit applies to every language-bound candidate, Cărtărescu included, and that it should not be applied selectively. She also says the citation should avoid claims of completeness or encyclopedic mastery.
responses.response: I agree that the translation limit must be applied symmetrically. If it lowers confidence in Adonis, it lowers confidence in Cărtărescu by the same logic. That is why I list it as a shared uncertainty and not as a reason against one writer in particular. It follows that the committee should seek informed readers of Romanian and Arabic, and treat their testimony as stronger than ours. I also take her point on the citation wording and have kept the revised version free of completeness claims. My own doubt about Adonis concerns whether the late work sustains the level of the early and middle poetry. That is an impression I hold at second hand, and I would withdraw it if Arabic readers disagreed. It does not by itself make him a weaker candidate than Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Mattson says a fair assessment must rest on the full oeuvre and not only the best-known long books. She would build the citation mainly on the prose and mention poetry only if enough of it can be read. She ranks Michon second for concentrated formal intensity, while accepting the breadth question.
responses.response: I follow her on the citation. The revised wording rests on the prose and names the poetry only as its lyric root, which is the most the translated evidence supports. I also agree that the judgment must go beyond Blinding and Solenoid, and I cannot supply the missing volumes myself. On Michon, my disagreement with her is still about the breadth criterion and not about quality. His compressed French prose is a real formal achievement, and a small corpus can be a complete one. A whole-oeuvre citation still needs evidence of sustained range, and a small corpus gives less of it. His effect also lies in syntax and register, so translation loss weighs on him more heavily than on the other candidates. For that reason I keep Carson and Adonis, not Michon, as the alternatives.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg proposes a citation that refers to a lifetime's work and to roots in Romanian poetry. He accepts the poetry-coverage gap as a limit on how much weight poetry can carry in the citation, and does not think it justifies dropping poetry. He keeps Carson as a serious alternative, with the question of how much of her work is original.
responses.response: I agree that the poetry should not be dropped, and my wording keeps it as the root of the prose. I would not use 'a lifetime's work' or the claim about Romanian poetry as a base, for the reason Palm and Carlberg give: the translated evidence we hold does not show it. The words can be restored if readers of the original confirm them. On Carson, we agree that the task is to establish what original work carries the case. Whether the committee settles that, and whether it treats her hybrid mode as central or specialized, matters more to the comparison with B043 than any count of positions.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement survives translation, and how uniform the quality is across the long, digressive novels. I cannot say from public knowledge which later volumes best show sustained quality.
Coverage of his poetry and essays in translation is thinner than for the novels, so the whole-oeuvre judgment is partial. This is why the citation names poetry only as the lyric root.

Whether the inward, maximalist mode amounts to breadth of significance or a narrower achievement. The evidence in the files is descriptive, and no member has read enough of the whole corpus to settle it.

Whether Carson's hybrid, scholarly and book-object work counts as a central or a specialized literary achievement, how translations and adaptations should be weighed, and how the will's wording bears on it.
Whether the late work of Adonis sustains the level of his earlier poetry. I hold this impression at second hand, and Arabic readers or expert reports could overturn it.
All assessments rest on general public knowledge and on colleagues' statements. I have not independently verified any text, and I make no claim about actual nominations or confidential proceedings.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, and unchanged since round 1. The profile records scholarly and editorial work on modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature and Celan, and service as committee chair. That is background context and not a personal, translation, editorial or institutional connection to any shortlisted writer. The chair summary disclosed that my opening ranking placed Carson first and Cărtărescu second and that I revised it in round 1. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
